title: Compiler Settings, Build Configurations and Undefined Behavior
summary: Turn compiler **warnings** up and read them. Build in **Debug** while you work and **Release** when you finish. And meet the most important phrase in C++: **undefined behaviour**.
markdown:
## The compiler has settings So far you have pressed Run and let the compiler get on with it. It has a few settings that matter, and Xenon has already chosen sensible ones. This lesson explains what they are, so they are not a mystery when you set up your own tools one day. ## Warnings: the compiler's advice An **error** means "I cannot build this". A **warning** means "I can build this, but it looks like a mistake". ```cpp #include int main() { int total{ 10 }; int count{ 3 }; int unused{ 5 }; std::cout << total / count << '\n'; return 0; } ``` This builds and runs. With warnings turned up, the compiler also tells you that `unused` is never used. Perhaps you meant to use it and forgot. | | Error | Warning | |---|---|---| | Does the program build? | No | Yes | | Should you fix it? | You have to | Yes, nearly always | > [!tip] Treat warnings as errors > Xenon compiles at a high warning level and shows warnings in the **Problems** tab. Some tasks are marked *strict*: they only pass when there are no warnings at all. That is how professional teams work, and it is a good habit to start now. ## Debug and Release The same source code can be built in two ways. ```mermaid flowchart LR SRC["Your code"] --> DBG["Debug build
extra safety checks
slower"] SRC --> REL["Release build
optimised
fast"] DBG --> D1["Use while writing
and fixing"] REL --> R1["Use for the
finished program"] ``` | | Debug | Release | |---|---|---| | Speed | Slower | Often many times faster | | Extra checks for mistakes | Yes | No | | Use it when | You are still working | You are finished, or measuring speed | In an **optimised** build the compiler rearranges your code to run faster while producing the same results. Xenon uses Debug unless you change it, because the extra checks catch mistakes. You can switch in **Settings**. ## Which version of C++? C++ is revised every three years, and a compiler has to be told which version to follow. Xenon uses the newest. If you copy code from an old tutorial and it looks different from what you learn here, a different version is usually the reason. ## Undefined behaviour This is the single most important idea in the lesson. Most languages stop you when you do something senseless. C++ often does not. For certain mistakes, the rules of the language simply **do not say** what happens. That is called **undefined behaviour**, usually shortened to **UB**. ```mermaid flowchart TD UB["Code with undefined behaviour"] --> A["Seems to work
(the worst outcome:
the mistake stays hidden)"] UB --> B["Wrong answer"] UB --> C["Crash"] UB --> D["Works today,
breaks tomorrow"] ``` You have already met one example: ```cpp int score; // never given a value std::cout << score << '\n'; // undefined behaviour ``` This might print 0. It might print 32767. It might print something different on another computer or after an unrelated change. All of those are "allowed", because the rules promise nothing. > [!danger] "It works on my machine" proves nothing > Code with undefined behaviour can pass every test you run and still be wrong. The only safe approach is to know the rules and not break them. The Debug build's extra checks catch some cases for you, which is one more reason to use it. ### The ones you will meet in this course | Mistake | Covered in | |---|---| | Reading a variable that was never given a value | [[1.04 Variables and Initialization]] | | A whole number growing too large for its type | [[2.02 Integers]] | | Dividing a whole number by zero | [[2.03 Floating Point Numbers]] | | Reading past the end of a list | [[5.01 std::vector Basics]] | | Following a pointer that points at nothing | [[4.04 Pointers]] | | Using something after it has been destroyed | [[7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory]] | You do not need to understand these yet. Just notice the pattern: each is something a careful programmer checks for. The complete picture comes much later, in [[13.01 Undefined Behavior and Object Lifetime]]. ## Words you cannot use as names C++ reserves about ninety words for itself, called **keywords**. You have used several already: `int`, `double`, `return`, `void`, `true`, `false`. You cannot name a variable or a function with one of them. The editor shows keywords in their own colour, so if a name you chose changes colour, pick another. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the difference between an error and a warning? - A warning stops the build; an error only gives advice + An error stops the build; a warning flags a likely mistake - Errors are about spelling; warnings are about maths - There is none; both stop the build > An **error** means the code is not valid C++ and the build stops. A **warning** lets the build finish but flags something that is probably a mistake. ? What does undefined behaviour mean? - The program will always crash straight away - The compiler refuses to build the program - The program prints a message saying what went wrong + The rules of C++ say nothing about what happens, so the result can be anything > With undefined behaviour the program might work, give a wrong answer or crash, and it can change between runs or computers. The compiler often does not stop it. ? Why is "it printed the right answer" not proof that code is correct? - Because the screen might show the wrong output + Code with undefined behaviour can appear to work by luck - Because the compiler only checks the first run - Because Release builds always print different answers > Undefined behaviour gives no guarantee. Code can look right today and fail on another run, computer or compiler setting. ? When would you use a Release build? - While writing and fixing the program, for its extra checks - Only when the Debug build will not compile + For the finished program, or when measuring how fast it runs - To get more warnings from the compiler > Release is optimized for speed. While writing and fixing code, Debug is better because of its extra checks and easier debugging. ```
ideas:
1. Run the warning example above and find the warning in the Problems tab. Then remove the unused variable.
2. In Settings, switch between Debug and Release and run any program in each.
3. Write a program that prints a variable you never gave a value. Run it a few times. Then fix it and never do it again.

cards.q: What is the difference between an error and a warning?
cards.a:
An error stops the build; a warning flags a likely mistake

An **error** means the code is not valid C++ and the build stops. A **warning** lets the build finish but flags something that is probably a mistake.

The rules of C++ say nothing about what happens, so the result can be anything

With undefined behaviour the program might work, give a wrong answer or crash, and it can change between runs or computers. The compiler often does not stop it.

cards.q: Why is "it printed the right answer" not proof that code is correct?
cards.a:
Code with undefined behaviour can appear to work by luck

Undefined behaviour gives no guarantee. Code can look right today and fail on another run, computer or compiler setting.

cards.q: When would you use a Release build?
cards.a:
For the finished program, or when measuring how fast it runs

Release is optimized for speed. While writing and fixing code, Debug is better because of its extra checks and easier debugging.
